title: Eigenvalues, characteristic equation, diagonalization
summary: Eigenvectors are the directions a matrix only stretches. Finding eigenvalues from det(A − λI) = 0, eigenspaces from Nul(A − λI), and deciding whether A = PDP⁻¹ (and using it to compute Aᵏ) is one of the most heavily tested skills on the final.

blocks.text: A nonzero vector x with Ax = λx for some scalar λ. λ is then an eigenvalue of A (λ = 0 is allowed; x = 0 is not).
Geometrically: A just stretches x (by λ) without turning it off its line. These are the directions in which A acts like a number, which is what makes powers Aᵏ easy.

blocks.name: λ is an eigenvalue ⇔ A − λI is singular
blocks.text: Ax = λx ⇔ (A − λI)x = 0. A nonzero solution exists ⇔ A − λI is not invertible ⇔ det(A − λI) = 0.

proof.text: Rewrite Ax − λx = 0 as (A − λI)x = 0 (note λI, not λ alone). Nontrivial null space ⇔ singular (IMT).

blocks.text: For an eigenvalue λ, the eigenspace is Nul(A − λI): all eigenvectors for λ together with 0. It is a subspace.

blocks.title: Verify an eigenvector / eigenvalue
blocks.prompt: A = [1 6; 5 2]. Are u = (6, −5) and v = (3, −2) eigenvectors? Is 7 an eigenvalue?
steps: Av = (3 − 12, 15 − 4) = (−9, 11), not a multiple of (3, −2): v is not an eigenvector.
A − 7I = [−6 6; 5 −5] has dependent columns ⇒ singular ⇒ 7 is an eigenvalue. Solve: x₁ = x₂, eigenvector (1, 1). Check A(1, 1) = (7, 7). ✓
blocks.answer: u is an eigenvector (λ = −4); v is not; 7 is an eigenvalue with eigenvector (1, 1).

blocks.name: Triangular matrices
blocks.text: The eigenvalues of a triangular matrix are its diagonal entries.

proof.text: A − λI is triangular with diagonal aᵢᵢ − λ; its det is ∏(aᵢᵢ − λ), zero exactly when λ = some aᵢᵢ.

blocks.name: Distinct eigenvalues ⇒ independent eigenvectors
blocks.text: Eigenvectors v₁, …, vᵣ for distinct eigenvalues λ₁, …, λᵣ are linearly independent.

proof.text: Suppose not; take the first vₚ₊₁ that is a combination c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₚvₚ of earlier independent ones. Apply A: λₚ₊₁vₚ₊₁ = Σcᵢλᵢvᵢ. Subtract λₚ₊₁ times the original: 0 = Σcᵢ(λᵢ − λₚ₊₁)vᵢ. Independence gives cᵢ(λᵢ − λₚ₊₁) = 0, and λᵢ ≠ λₚ₊₁, so all cᵢ = 0, making vₚ₊₁ = 0, impossible.

blocks.text: det(A − λI), a polynomial of degree n in λ. Its roots (the solutions of the characteristic equation det(A − λI) = 0) are the eigenvalues.
The multiplicity of λ as a root of the characteristic polynomial.
2×2: det(A − λI) = λ² − (tr A)λ + det A

blocks.name: Trace and determinant
blocks.text: Counting complex roots with multiplicity, the product of the eigenvalues is det A and their sum is tr A (sum of diagonal entries). In particular 0 is an eigenvalue ⇔ det A = 0 ⇔ A is singular.

blocks.title: Characteristic polynomial of a 3×3
blocks.prompt: Find the characteristic polynomial and eigenvalues of B = [2 0 0; 1 2 1; −1 0 1].
steps: Expand along row 1 (two zeros): (2 − λ)·det [2−λ 1; 0 1−λ] = (2 − λ)(2 − λ)(1 − λ).

blocks.text: Row reduction changes eigenvalues. Never row reduce A before finding eigenvalues; you may only row reduce A − λI to find eigenvectors once λ is known.

blocks.title: Eigenspace basis
items: For each eigenvalue λ, form A − λI (subtract λ down the diagonal).
Row reduce and solve (A − λI)x = 0 in parametric vector form.
The free-variable vectors form a basis of the eigenspace. Its dimension is the geometric multiplicity = n − rank(A − λI).

blocks.name: Geometric ≤ algebraic
blocks.text: For each eigenvalue, 1 ≤ dim(eigenspace) ≤ algebraic multiplicity.

blocks.title: Eigenspace with a repeated eigenvalue
blocks.prompt: A = [4 −1 6; 2 1 6; 2 −1 8] has characteristic polynomial −(λ − 9)(λ − 2)². Find a basis for each eigenspace.
steps: λ = 9: A − 9I = [−5 −1 6; 2 −8 6; 2 −1 −1]. Row sums are 0, so (1, 1, 1) is in the null space; rank 2 ⇒ basis (1, 1, 1).

blocks.text: A and B are similar if B = P⁻¹AP for some invertible P.

blocks.name: Similar matrices share the characteristic polynomial
blocks.text: Hence the same eigenvalues with the same multiplicities, the same determinant, trace and rank. (Not the same eigenvectors.)

proof.text: det(P⁻¹AP − λI) = det(P⁻¹(A − λI)P) = det P⁻¹ · det(A − λI) · det P = det(A − λI).

blocks.text: A = PDP⁻¹ with D diagonal.

blocks.name: Diagonalization Theorem
blocks.text: An n×n matrix A is diagonalizable ⇔ A has n linearly independent eigenvectors. Then the columns of P are those eigenvectors and the diagonal entries of D are the corresponding eigenvalues, in the same order.

proof.text: AP = A[v₁ ⋯ vₙ] = [λ₁v₁ ⋯ λₙvₙ] = PD. P is invertible exactly when its columns are independent, and then A = PDP⁻¹. Conversely AP = PD read column by column says each column of P is an eigenvector.

blocks.name: Tests
blocks.text: (1) n distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalizable (sufficient, not necessary). (2) A is diagonalizable ⇔ for every eigenvalue, geometric multiplicity = algebraic multiplicity (and the characteristic polynomial factors fully over ℝ), i.e. the eigenspace dimensions add to n.

Why distinct eigenvalues suffice: one eigenvector each, and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent, so n of them form a basis. A repeated eigenvalue decides nothing by itself: you must check whether its eigenspace is big enough. I (eigenvalue 1 repeated) is diagonal; [1 1; 0 1] (eigenvalue 1 repeated) is not diagonalizable.

blocks.title: Diagonalize A
items: Find a basis of each eigenspace.
If the total number of basis vectors is n, put them as columns of P and the matching eigenvalues on the diagonal of D. Otherwise A is not diagonalizable.

blocks.title: Diagonalize a 3×3
blocks.prompt: Diagonalize A = [1 3 3; −3 −5 −3; 3 3 1], given its characteristic polynomial −(λ − 1)(λ + 2)².

blocks.title: Prove a matrix is not diagonalizable
blocks.prompt: Show A = [2 4 3; −4 −6 −3; 3 3 1] is not diagonalizable (its characteristic polynomial is also −(λ − 1)(λ + 2)²). Also explain [1 1; 0 1].
steps: Only 1 + 1 = 2 independent eigenvectors in total, fewer than 3.
[1 1; 0 1]: eigenvalue 1 twice, but A − I = [0 1; 0 0] has rank 1, so only one independent eigenvector (1, 0).
blocks.answer: Not diagonalizable: geometric multiplicity of −2 is 1 but algebraic is 2. Same for [1 1; 0 1] with λ = 1.

blocks.text: A 2×2 matrix with a repeated eigenvalue λ is diagonalizable only if it already equals λI.

blocks.name: Powers
blocks.text: If A = PDP⁻¹ then Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹, and Dᵏ just raises each diagonal entry to the k-th power.

proof.text: A² = PDP⁻¹PDP⁻¹ = PD²P⁻¹; the inner P⁻¹P cancel, and so on by induction.

blocks.text: To compute Aᵏx for one vector, skip P⁻¹: write x = c₁v₁ + ⋯ + cₙvₙ in eigenvectors; then Aᵏx = c₁λ₁ᵏv₁ + ⋯ + cₙλₙᵏvₙ. As k → ∞ the term with the largest |λ| dominates.

blocks.title: Similar or not?
blocks.prompt: (a) Are [1 2; 3 4] and [0 1; 2 5] similar? (b) Are [1 1; 0 1] and I similar?
steps: (a) Both have trace 5 and det −2, so both have characteristic polynomial λ² − 5λ − 2, with discriminant 25 + 8 = 33 > 0: two distinct real eigenvalues. Each is similar to the same diagonal matrix, hence to each other.
(b) Same characteristic polynomial (λ − 1)², but P⁻¹IP = I for every P, so the only matrix similar to I is I itself.
blocks.answer: (a) Similar. (b) Not similar (same eigenvalues are not enough).

blocks.title: Six True/False
blocks.prompt: (a) A diagonalizable matrix is invertible. (b) An invertible matrix is diagonalizable. (c) A 3×3 matrix with 3 distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable. (d) A and Aᵀ have the same eigenvalues. (e) If A is diagonalizable, its eigenvalues are distinct. (f) The sum of two eigenvectors is an eigenvector.
steps: (d) True: det(Aᵀ − λI) = det((A − λI)ᵀ) = det(A − λI) (but eigenvectors can differ).
(e) False: I is diagonal with eigenvalue 1 repeated.
(f) False in general: eigenvectors for different eigenvalues don't add to an eigenvector (and v + (−v) = 0 is not one).
blocks.answer: (a) F (b) F (c) T (d) T (e) F (f) F

blocks.text: Diagonalizable is about having enough eigenvectors; invertible is about 0 not being an eigenvalue. They are independent properties.

back.text: Ax = λx with x ≠ 0. λ may be 0; x may not.

cards.front: How do you check if λ is an eigenvalue?

back.text: Check whether A − λI is singular (det(A − λI) = 0, or row reduce and look for a free variable).

cards.front: How do you verify that u is an eigenvector?

back.text: Compute Au and see whether it is a scalar multiple of u; the multiple is the eigenvalue.
Nul(A − λI): the eigenvectors for λ plus 0. Its dimension is the geometric multiplicity.
λ² − (tr A)λ + det A.
Its diagonal entries.
Sum = trace; product = det (with multiplicity, complex included).
A is singular (det A = 0, Nul A ≠ {0}).
No. Find eigenvalues from det(A − λI) of the original A.
Algebraic: multiplicity as a root of det(A − λI). Geometric: dim Nul(A − λI) = n − rank(A − λI). Always 1 ≤ geometric ≤ algebraic.
A = PDP⁻¹ ⇔ A has n independent eigenvectors; P's columns are eigenvectors, D's diagonal the matching eigenvalues.

cards.front: Why does having n distinct eigenvalues guarantee diagonalizability?

back.text: One eigenvector per eigenvalue, and eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent: n independent eigenvectors.

cards.front: Does a repeated eigenvalue mean not diagonalizable?

back.text: No. I has a repeated eigenvalue and is diagonal. You must check that each eigenspace dimension equals the algebraic multiplicity.

cards.front: A 2×2 matrix that is not diagonalizable, and why?

back.text: [1 1; 0 1]: eigenvalue 1 twice, but A − I = [0 1; 0 0] has rank 1, so only one independent eigenvector.
Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹, Dᵏ = diag(λ₁ᵏ, …, λₙᵏ).
Write x = Σcᵢvᵢ in eigenvectors; Aᵏx = Σcᵢλᵢᵏvᵢ.
Characteristic polynomial, eigenvalues with multiplicities, det, trace, rank, eigenspace dimensions. Not eigenvectors.
No: [1 1; 0 1] and I have the same eigenvalues but are not similar. (True if both are diagonalizable.)
Independent properties: diag(0, 1) is diagonalizable but singular; [1 1; 0 1] is invertible but not diagonalizable.

cards.front: If Ax = λx, what are A²x and A⁻¹x?

back.text: λ²x; λ⁻¹x (if A invertible, so λ ≠ 0).
0 and 1 (λ² = λ).

cards.front: Check a diagonalization without inverting P?

back.text: Verify AP = PD column by column.

solution.text: Expand det(A − λI) along column 2: (3 − λ)[(4−λ)² − 1] = (3 − λ)(3 − λ)(5 − λ). Eigenvalues 3 (double), 5.
, D = diag(3, 3, 5), A = PDP⁻¹. (Geometric = algebraic multiplicity for λ = 3, so diagonalizable.)
What it tests: Repeated eigenvalue ≠ not diagonalizable: check the rank of A − λI. For Aⁿx, expand x in eigenvectors instead of computing P⁻¹.

hard.title: Diagonalizability with parameters

prompt.text: , classify by a: two distinct real eigenvalues / one repeated / complex. When is B diagonalizable over ℝ?

hard.answer: (a) h = 0 (b) |a| > 2 distinct real (diagonalizable), a = ±2 repeated (not), |a| < 2 complex; diagonalizable over ℝ iff |a| > 2

solution.text: : rank 1 if h = 0 (rows (0,0,1) twice), rank 2 otherwise. Diagonalizable ⇔ h = 0.
|a| > 2: two distinct real ⇒ diagonalizable over ℝ. |a| < 2: complex pair, not diagonalizable over ℝ (but is over ℂ).
a = ±2: λ = ±1 repeated; B ≠ λI, so the eigenspace is 1-D ⇒ not diagonalizable. Answer: |a| > 2.
What it tests: A 2×2 matrix with a repeated eigenvalue is diagonalizable only if it is already λI. In (a) the 1 in the corner is irrelevant; only h matters.

prompt.text: (a) Find the 2×2 matrix with eigenvalues 2 and −1 and corresponding eigenvectors (1, 1) and (1, 2). (b) Find a formula for its k-th power.

solution.text: What it tests: Order matters: the i-th column of P must match the i-th diagonal entry of D. Sanity-check with trace and determinant.

hard.title: Eigenvalues of A², A⁻¹, idempotents

prompt.text: (a) If Ax = λx with x ≠ 0, show A²x = λ²x, and if A is invertible, A⁻¹x = λ⁻¹x. (b) Deduce: if A² = A, every eigenvalue is 0 or 1.

hard.answer: A²x = λ²x, A⁻¹x = λ⁻¹x; λ² = λ ⇒ λ ∈ {0, 1}

solution.title: Solution
items: If A is invertible, λ ≠ 0 (else Ax = 0 with x ≠ 0). Apply A⁻¹ to Ax = λx: x = λA⁻¹x ⇒ A⁻¹x = λ⁻¹x.

solution.text: What it tests: Use x ≠ 0 explicitly when cancelling. This polynomial trick works for any equation p(A) = 0.

prompt.text: A is 4×4 with characteristic polynomial λ²(λ − 1)². (a) If rank A = 3, is A diagonalizable? (b) If rank A = 2, can you decide? (c) If rank A = 2 and rank(A − I) = 2?

solution.text: dim of the 0-eigenspace = dim Nul A = 4 − rank A.
(a) dim Nul A = 1 < 2 = algebraic multiplicity of 0 ⇒ not diagonalizable.
(b) 0-eigenspace has dim 2 (good), but the 1-eigenspace could be 1- or 2-dimensional: cannot decide. Example of each: diag(0,0,1,1) vs. 0 ⊕ 0 ⊕
What it tests: Every eigenvalue must pass “geometric = algebraic”. Rank of A only speaks about λ = 0.

prompt.text: A real 3×3 matrix has det A = 6, trace A = 6, and 1 is an eigenvalue. Find all eigenvalues. Is A diagonalizable? Is A − 2I invertible?

solution.title: Solution
items: λ₁λ₂λ₃ = 6, λ₁ + λ₂ + λ₃ = 6, λ₁ = 1 ⇒ λ₂ + λ₃ = 5, λ₂λ₃ = 6 ⇒ λ² − 5λ + 6 = 0 ⇒ 2, 3.

solution.text: What it tests: det = product and trace = sum of eigenvalues (with multiplicity, complex included).

prompt.text: T: ℙ₂ → ℙ₂, T(p)(t) = p(t + 1). Find the matrix of T relative to {1, t, t²}, its eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and show T is not diagonalizable.

hard.answer: Matrix [1 1 1; 0 1 2; 0 0 1]; only eigenvalue 1, eigenvectors the constants; not diagonalizable

solution.text: has rank 2 ⇒ eigenspace dim 1: only the constant polynomials.
One independent eigenvector in a 3-D space ⇒ not diagonalizable. (Makes sense: p(t+1) = λp(t) forces p constant.)
What it tests: Eigenvectors of a map on ℙ₂ are polynomials. Translate to coordinates, solve, and translate back.
